/api/help/crew.title: Signing up as crew
/api/help/crew.summary: Commentating or tracking a match, from signing up and getting approved through confirming and withdrawing.

headings.text: Signing up before a match is booked

spans.text: Crew covers the two jobs behind a streamed match. Commentators talk over the match on stream. Trackers run the item and progress tracking viewers see next to the game, the overlay showing what each player has found and how far along they are.
Some events add a third job,
Broadcaster
: running the stream for that match. It only shows up where staff have turned it on.
They all work the same way: sign up, get approved, confirm, turn up. Anyone in the community can do it, and you don't need a volunteer role.
Signing up
Open Event, stay on the Schedule view, and turn on
Needs crew
. That hides every match that's already covered or under way, which on a busy day is most of the board. Then tap
Sign up
in the match's Commentators or Trackers column. On a phone each role sits under the match name with its own button,
Sign up as commentator
or
Sign up as tracker
There's no confirm step. If you tapped the wrong one,
Withdraw
is in the same spot.
Signing up tells staff you're available for that slot. A staff member decides who actually gets it.
Every streamed match has commentary. Some tournaments don't use trackers, and for those the Trackers column is empty on purpose.
A match that still needs crew: tap
Sign up as commentator
(1) or
Sign up as tracker

blocks.alt: A match on the board on a phone: Racer Five vs Racer Six on Stage 3, Commentary 0/1 and Tracking 0/1 both marked needs crew, with Sign up as commentator marked 1 and Sign up as tracker marked 2

spans.text: If you can't sign up, the
Sign up
button is greyed out with the reason next to it.

items.text: You're playing
means it's your own match, and you can't crew your own game.
Signups closed
means the match has started. Signups close when a proctor starts it. A match that's only checked in is still open, since that's exactly when a stream finds out it's short a commentator.

spans.text: If you've already signed up for that role on that match, you'll see
Withdraw
instead.
Signing up before a match is booked
Want the final while the semifinals haven't been played? Open
Not scheduled yet
at the bottom of Event › Schedule. It lists every bracket match nobody has booked a time for, with the sides it's still waiting on ("Andy or Benny", "Winner of C", "TBD"). Sign up there the same way.

Your signup waits on the match. When it gets booked, your signup moves onto the booking, approved or not, and the match shows up on your list with its time. Staff can approve you before then. If you turn out to be busy at the time it's booked for, the staff who approve crew get told so they can sort it out.
You won't get a new DM when it's booked. As with every match, you hear about it once it's on a stage. If you end up playing in it, your crew signup is dropped.
Commentating as a pair
On a match that needs two commentators, sign up first, then tap
Invite a partner
next to your
Withdraw
and pick who you want on the mic with you. They get a Discord DM with
Decline
and
Accept
, and the same pair under Commentary invites at the top of My Schedule.
Until they answer, your tray says who you invited, with
Cancel invite
if you change your mind. Once they accept, they're signed up as commentator with "with
your name
" beside them. You get one partner per match.

Staff still approve each of you on their own, so they can take one of you and not the other. If you withdraw, a partner who already accepted stays signed up, and an invite nobody has answered yet is cancelled.
Signing up from Discord
If you follow a tournament, the DM announcing each new match has
Sign up as Commentator
and
Sign up as Tracker
buttons. They do the same thing as
Sign up
on the board. The DM's
View the schedule
button opens the board if you want to see who's playing first.
You pick which tournaments DM you, and how much, under Profile → Notifications → Tournaments you follow.
Notifications and Discord DMs
explains the levels. Most crew want
Streamed, plus possible streams
, which covers matches with a stage and the ones staff are thinking about streaming.
Getting approved

Staff have the final say on every crew slot. A staff member, the tournament's admin or its crew coordinator decides who covers each one. Signing up puts your name forward but doesn't reserve anything.
It isn't first come, first served. Staff can see what else you're doing at that time, including matches you're playing in, and a clash is the usual reason a signup gets passed over.
Staff get a Discord DM as soon as you sign up. When they approve you, you get a DM too, with an
Acknowledge
button and a
View your crew slot
button that opens your slot on My Schedule.
Staff can also put you on a match you never signed up for. You get the same DM, and the slot shows up on My Schedule ready to confirm.

They can withdraw an approval, right up to the day of the match, if plans for the stream change or someone better suited frees up. You'll get a DM, your confirmation is cleared, and you go back to waiting for approval. If they take you off the match completely, it disappears from your list. Neither is a judgement on you.
Confirming
Once you're approved, you still need to confirm you can cover the slot. Until you do, staff can't tell whether you've seen the approval.
You can confirm in any of these places, and they all do the same thing:

items.text: Confirm
, next to
Withdraw
in your role's column on My Schedule
the same
Confirm
on the schedule board
Acknowledge
, on the DM you were sent

spans.text: My Schedule

Crew you signed up for, on Home's My Schedule tab, is the schedule board cut down to the matches you're crewing. If you aren't playing in any tournament it's at the top of the tab. If you are, it comes after your own matches. Each line looks the same as on the schedule, with your
Withdraw
(and
Confirm
, once you're approved) in your role's column, so the names tell you where you stand:

rows.text: You've signed up. Staff haven't decided yet.
You have the slot. Confirm that you can still cover it.
You have the slot and you've confirmed. Nothing left to do.

spans.text: Finished matches drop off. Add
Finished
and
Confirmed
to the State filter to see the ones you've already worked.
Crew you signed up for, on My Schedule.

blocks.alt: Crew you signed up for on a phone: a live match where your tracking signup is waiting for approval, a match where you have the commentary slot with Withdraw as commentator and Confirm, and tomorrow's match where your commentary signup is waiting

spans.text: Reading the crew columns

The board has a Commentators column and a Trackers column. Each starts with approved crew against what the match needs, so "1/2" means one approved commentator out of two. People still waiting for approval don't count, so a match can have three signups and still say "needs crew".
Needs crew

uses the same rule to decide whether a match is covered. Crew only works matches on a stage, so a match with no stage yet just shows how many have signed up and never says "needs crew". On a phone, each card names the role instead ("Commentary 1/2").
Your own
Sign up
or
Withdraw
sits in a shaded box under the count, in the same place on every match. When there's nothing you can do, the button is greyed out with the reason, like "Signups closed" or "You're playing".
The names come after that. A tick means approved, and a clock with "waiting for approval" means not yet. Your own name has "(you)" after it. "No signups yet" means nobody's asked for that slot.
Withdrawing
Withdraw
takes you off a slot. You can do it from My Schedule or the schedule board, before or after approval, even once the match has started.

Withdrawing before anyone's approved you costs nobody anything. Withdrawing from a slot you were approved for means staff have to find cover, so they're told right away, and the app warns you about that before you confirm.
If you'd already confirmed, withdrawing clears that too. Do it as early as you can.
If nobody approves you

Signups wait until staff get to them, which at a busy event might be shortly before the match. If a match you signed up for has started and you never heard back, the slot went to someone else. You can withdraw the old signup or leave it. Either way it drops off your list once the match ends.
On the day
Where to be and when, who runs the countdown and how a stage works are up to the event, not the app. If your community publishes them, they're under Event Guide in the sidebar.

/api/event-info/schedule.title: What's on, and when
/api/event-info/schedule.summary: Dates, room hours, the on-site tournaments, prize pools and your own match times.

spans.text: SpeedGaming Live 2026 runs Thursday 22 to Sunday 25 October at the DoubleTree by Hilton Washington Dulles Airport in Herndon, Virginia. All times here are Eastern Daylight Time (EDT, UTC−4), the venue's local time.
Hours
Doors open Thursday 22 October at 8 AM. Wednesday is for getting in and picking up your badge.

rows.text: 8 AM to midnight Thursday to Saturday, 8 AM to 6 PM Sunday
Piedmont I + II, 2nd floor, above the fitness center
4 to 10 PM Wednesday, 10 AM to 8 PM Thursday and Friday, 10 AM to 4 PM Saturday
Old Ox on Wednesday, Colvin Thursday to Monday

spans.text: Pick a match time that lets you finish before the room closes, and remember Sunday wraps up at 6 PM. Suggest a time in the app already sticks to these hours. If you need to play after close, that has to be cleared with SGL staff ahead of time. Tournament admins can't approve it.
The casual room is for pick-up races, side events and practice, and one of its rooms hosts the Best of NES High Score Challenge. The tournament room is only for scheduled matches.
On-site tournaments
Each tournament's rules have its settings. You'll see a Sign up button while a tournament is still taking entries.
A few have something extra first:

items.text: A Link to the Past Randomizer Glitched (HMG) has an async qualifier, open from Friday 16 October until noon on Thursday 22 October.
A Link to the Past any% runs qualifier races on site. The times are in its rules.
For the Best of NES High Score Challenge, check in at the Best of NES room.

spans.text: Most tournaments play groups on Thursday and Friday, then brackets on Saturday and Sunday. You and your opponent schedule group matches yourselves once groups are out. Bracket matches are scheduled for you, and you'll get a DM when yours is ready.
Prize pools
Prize pools come from community contributions plus a bonus from SpeedGaming, which doesn't take a cut. To chip in,
contribute on Matcherino
and put the game's name in the comment, plus whether it's for on-site or online.
Your own times
My Schedule shows your matches and Schedule shows everyone's, both in your own time zone. You'll also get a Discord DM whenever one of your matches is scheduled, moved or cancelled.

If a time doesn't work for you, use Ask to change on My Schedule, and ask early. Once a match has a stage and crew, it's a lot harder to move. Until staff reply, plan on the original time. If it's the day of the match, skip the request and find an admin in the tournament room.
Watching
The four stages are in the broadcast room, with seats for the audience. They stream on
twitch.tv/SpeedGaming
and
twitch.tv/SpeedGaming2
, and Watch in the side menu shows what's on each one. The tournament room isn't streamed and isn't open to spectators.
Online tournaments
The online side of SGLive is free to enter and runs on its own dates. You'll find the list on
sglive.speedgaming.org

items.text: An archived event is read-only: its pages say so under the title, its add buttons and ⋮ menus are gone, and anything that tries to change it is turned away. Staff can unarchive it from the same notice.
Archiving an event closes its open race rooms, drops seed rolls still waiting, and takes back the Discord roles its rules gave.
Emergency contacts and accommodation requests for an archived event are deleted 30 days after it was archived.

Matches can have broadcasters as well as commentators and trackers. Staff turn them on per event under Event settings → Crew; anyone in the community can then sign up from the schedule or the crew DM, and staff approve them the same way. Each tournament sets how many it needs (1 by default, 0 for none), and the boards, match editor and crew report gain a Broadcasters column.
Commentators and trackers can sign up for bracket matches nobody has booked yet, like a final whose players aren't decided. They're under
Not scheduled yet
at the bottom of Event › Schedule. When the match is booked the signups move onto it, approvals included, and staff hear if an approved person is busy at the booked time.
The REST API and the Wizzrobe MCP connector work in any event: pass
event
with its link name (
?event=sgl27
, or an
event
argument on a tool), or leave it out for the default event. A call about one match or shift works in that row's own event. New
/api/events
routes and event tools list, create, copy, go live, archive and configure events, and
whoami
lists each community's events.
The audit log, sent messages and engagement telemetry can be narrowed to one event over the API and the connector.

Webhooks can be limited to some events: the webhook dialog's new From events choice is All events or Only these events, and each webhook's row names its events under the URL. The old Events field is now called Updates. Existing webhooks keep sending every event's updates, except SG Schedule Update, which sends SGL 2026's only.
A new staff help article, "Running more than one event", covers starting next year's event, going live, the default event and archiving. Its help icon is on Admin → Events.
A community can now run several events. Staff create, copy, take live, archive and set the default one under Admin → Events, and the event button beside the community name switches between them.
Each event has its own dates, hours, capacity, venue, timezone and volunteer reward tiers under Admin → Event settings.
My Schedule, My Shifts and Home › Tournaments show every live event you're in, with the event's name on a row once two events share the list, and links back to past events.

AI assistants connected to Wizzrobe can read a tournament's whole bracket in one go, for native, start.gg and Challonge brackets: every round and set, who feeds into what, scores, booked matches and standings. It's the same view anyone can already see on the bracket page.

A Link to the Past matches have an item tracker for restreams. The match's approved trackers, staff and broadcast techs open it from the match sheet, tap items and dungeons as the runner finds them, and see what viewers see after the stream delay. Each runner gets a transparent board to add to OBS as a browser source. Communities turn it on under Admin → Features.
Commentators can bring a partner. Sign up on a match that needs two commentators, tap
Invite a partner
, and the person you pick gets Accept and Decline on Discord and on My Schedule. Staff still approve each of you on your own.

Members can set up their own webhooks under Profile → Webhooks (when the community turns it on): up to three, sending their matches, crew signups, shifts and qualifier runs, or anything else they can see, to a Discord channel or their own app. Each message is checked against what they can see when it's sent, and staff-only details never go out.
On a restreamed match in a room the racetime bot runs, the seed now waits for the broadcaster. Once the match's approved broadcaster types
!ready
in the room, the seed goes out (at its usual time, or straight away if that's passed). If nobody has typed
!ready
by the start time, the bot says so in the room and DMs the broadcaster and on-duty staff, and staff can still send the seed with
!forceroll
. This only applies on events with Broadcasters turned on.
Online tournaments can let the racetime bot run their rooms: tick
Bot runs the room
under Racetime on the tournament. The bot invites the players, posts the seed and its code 10 minutes before the start (you pick the minutes), and answers
!seed
!forceroll
(monitors and staff) and
!fpa
(runners, which tells on-duty staff). Clean results record and go to the bracket on their own; a close finish, a forfeit, an FPA call or a runner it can't match waits for staff under
Racetime results held
in Needs you, with a Check result button. Players without racetime linked get a Link racetime button when their room opens, and staff see "not linked" on the match.

Players can release their own seed. Turn on "Players release their own seed" under a tournament's Seeds & randomizer settings, and once a proctor checks a match in, each player taps Ready for seed on My Schedule or on their check-in DM. The seed rolls and goes to everyone the moment the last player is ready, and anyone can take Ready back until then. Proctors and staff can still roll it whenever they like, and their boards show "1 of 2 ready" on the seed line.

Tournament admins now get a Discord DM the moment a match result comes in, with who won, the time or score, when it was played and where it was reported, including results reported straight on Challonge or start.gg. They arrive silently; change them under Notifications ("Result in").

Stream layouts: staff and Broadcast Techs can design each event's broadcast overlay under Admin → Stream Layouts (start from a stock layout on a plain colour, with the same box positions as the SGL SpeedGaming and FFR layouts, or upload your own art, then place player names, round, commentators, seed code, up next and more on it). Each stage gets an OBS link that follows the match on that stage, and you can download ready-made OBS scenes with every video hole wired to a shared feed, and a match can be pinned from its match sheet. Communities turn it on under Admin → Features once it's made available.

Outside apps can now sign you in with Wizzrobe, where a community has Third-party Apps turned on. One card shows who made the app, where it sends you and what it asks for: reads start ticked, changes start unticked, and it only ever works in the community you pick.
Apps you've connected sit with your API tokens on Profile, tagged App, and disconnect with one press. Profile also has a Developer apps section for registering an app of your own.
Staff can see which apps members connected under Admin → Settings → Connected apps, and block one for the whole community.

Help has a new article for developers, Building an app on Wizzrobe. It covers registering an app, the sign-in steps, what each permission reaches, limits and errors, plus an example script you can download and run.
Developers can try a read-only GraphQL API at
/api/graphql

with the same tokens as the REST API. It answers who you are and which events you can see for now; matches, tournaments and brackets come next. Open the address in a browser to explore it in GraphiQL.

The GraphQL API now reads tournaments, stages, the match schedule (players, approved crew, stage and seed, a page at a time) and each tournament's bracket, whether it runs in Wizzrobe, on start.gg or on Challonge.

Post-event surveys: staff build one under Admin → Surveys, starting from a template, and send it by DM to everyone who took part. Each person only gets the parts that fit what they did: one per tournament played, one per volunteer position, plus crew and check-in. Answers can be anonymous. Turn it on under Admin → Features.

Surveys can ask an agree scale: several statements, each answered from Strongly disagree to Strongly agree. It's a grid on a computer and one card per statement on a phone, and results show a bar per statement.

Staff can press Suggest questions on a draft survey section to get a few AI-drafted questions built from what happened at the event. The community uses its own Claude or OpenAI-compatible key under Settings → Integrations, nothing is sent until someone presses the button, and no names or anything people typed are ever sent.

Survey choice questions can add "Other" with a write-in box, a "None of these" answer that clears the other ticks, and a limit on how many people pick. Comments can be switched to a long answer with a character count.
Survey sections can have a short description, and commentators, trackers and broadcast crew can each get their own section.
Drag questions by their handle to reorder a survey, including into another section. On a phone, press and hold the handle first.

Survey questions can now show only to people who had a match on a stage, or played in the tournament room, in any tournament. Inside a per-tournament section, these look at the whole event rather than that one tournament.

Event › Schedule has a Friends switch: pick your friends once in the Friends filter and one tap shows only their matches, across every tournament. Your list is saved to your account, and friends' names are underlined on the board.
Surveys have a
Comments

tab: every comment and "Other" answer in one list, filtered by question, with search. Mark each one read and tag it (Wizzrobe, Venue, Schedule, Staff, Praise, or your own). Read marks and tags are shared by all staff, and the tag counts show what comes up most. People who answered never see them.
Survey results open with a drop-off card: how many people opened, started and sent the survey, which parts they reached, where the rest stopped, and the median time to finish against the estimate.
Survey invites and reminders have a
Not interested
button. Pressing it stops the reminders; the survey link still works.
An open survey's Actions menu has
Change close date…
Survey parts can be aimed at one volunteer position: "Worked one of these positions" lets you pick one or more positions, and "Volunteered (any position)" covers everyone with a shift.
Surveys now reach tournament organizers. A section can repeat for each tournament someone runs, and "Ran a tournament" asks organizers something once.
The Admin menu is split in two: what belongs to the event you're looking at, then what's the same across the community.
Community Events are now called Meetups.

Connecting an AI client like Claude now shows the same checklist as outside apps: pick what it can see and which changes it can make, instead of one read-or-write switch. Connections you've already made keep working as they are.

When a message link opens your crew slots, your matches or the admin Match Schedule on a single match, a "One match ✕" chip in the filter row says so; tap it to see everything again. Your Withdraw and Sign up buttons on crew cards lost the dashed box around them.

On-site roles (Proctor, Broadcast Tech, Triforce Submitter, Volunteer Coordinator, Equipment Manager, Volunteer and Check-in Desk) are now held in one event, so a proctor for this year's event isn't automatically one for next year's. Staff, Preset Manager, Sync Admin and Qualifier Admin still cover every event. Existing grants moved to each community's default event.

Edit member shows community-wide roles and roles in one event (pick the event beside the label), with a line naming what the person holds in other events. The Members list names the event for roles held elsewhere.
Discord role mappings for on-site roles name the event they grant in, the default event unless you pick another.
Seed DMs for A Link to the Past, AVIANART and Donkey Kong 64 now show the file-select code as the game's own icons, with the item names underneath.
Volunteer shift reminders and "Your shift is starting" DMs now say who you're taking over from and who's taking over from you at the end, on the same position.

The Running late button is now called "Tell staff I'm late", on My Schedule, the stage reminder DM and the volunteer shift-start DM. Two players read the old label as a status rather than a button. Once you've sent it, your match reads "Staff know: ~20 min".

Tournament filters on the match boards, Reports and Triforce Texts now show each tournament's short name (OoTR rather than Ocarina of Time Randomizer), so several picks fit on one line. Tournaments without a short name keep their full name.
Webhook messages now say which event they're from, with an
event
field holding its id, link name and name. Messages about the whole community have
event: null
A payout place can now be a fixed dollar amount instead of a percent, so splits announced in dollars (like $650 for first) record to the cent.
1–5 and 0–10 survey questions are now sliders, so they fit on a phone screen.
Surveys only count someone as crew if the match they crewed was on a stage.
The anonymous option now says plainly that what you write may still identify you.

Reporting a result is one tap: a live two-player match shows both names under "Who won?" on the board and in the match, and a short Undo replaces the confirm steps. A result staff or the tournament admin records is confirmed in the same tap.
Approving a commentator, tracker or broadcaster is one tap with Undo, and their DM waits until Undo runs out. Confirming a proctor's result is one tap with Undo too.
Sending a survey with a required question left blank now lists what's missing at the top, marks those parts, and jumps straight to each question.

The survey builder shows how long most people will take beside the longest path, plus a Checks list of things worth a second look, like a rating that asks two things at once or a part nobody will see.
The survey preview starts with a table of what each kind of person sees, and greys out what they won't see, with the reason.
A duplicated survey's results show last time's numbers under each carried question.
Survey DMs greet people by name and say how long their own survey takes. A reminder to someone who saved answers but never sent them says they're partway through.
A survey can send two reminders, and the second is worded as a last call.
The builder's "too long" warning now starts at 10 minutes instead of 5.
Survey results read in the survey's own sections, one line per question with a bar and its key number, so a big survey fits on a few screens instead of dozens.
A section asked once per tournament or volunteer position is a comparison table, and a tournament or position well below the rest is flagged.
Comments open in a side sheet with search and a chip per tournament or position.
Filter the whole results page to one tournament's players, one volunteer position, crew or people who checked in. Results also show the response rate for players, volunteers and crew.
After sending a survey, people see what happens next (staff can write their own line under Edit details) and whether their answers went anonymously.
Staff can fix a typo in a sent survey's wording with "Fix wording…" in each question's and section's ⋮. Questions reworded after answers came in are tagged "Edited" in results, with the old wording.

A Discord DM that doesn't go through because the bot is offline or Discord is having trouble is now tried again for up to 15 minutes, instead of being dropped. Sent messages shows it as pending until it lands.
The Match Schedule's "Needs you" list and "Not booked yet" view only show the event you're looking at.
An export started while looking at another event, or at an archived one, now exports that event's tournaments and volunteers instead of the default event's.
Match boards, tournament filters and other lists that refresh themselves (paging, switching tabs, the Refresh button) no longer fail with an error and stay empty.
The board's Approve button no longer resets to Approve when another match changes, which made the second tap look like it did nothing.
Closing a survey part with Back to parts, the close button or a tap outside now keeps what you typed, instead of only Done saving it.
Third-party apps now have a request ceiling shared by all their users, and you can register up to five new apps a day.
Apps that run in a browser can call Wizzrobe from the address they registered, and from nowhere else.
The API docs now list the scope a third-party app needs for each endpoint, ready for "Sign in with Wizzrobe". Personal API tokens work exactly as before.

Staff decide how every message Wizzrobe sends arrives (ping, silent or off) for each kind of recipient, under Admin → Notifications. On Profile → Notifications you pick Everything, Only what needs me or Quiet, adjust any single message, and can turn on sixteen extra ones that are off by default.
Messages sent to you, on Profile → Notifications, lists every message Wizzrobe sent you. The line at the bottom of each notification opens that exact message so you can change how you get it.

Staff can see every DM sent in the community and whether it arrived, under Admin → Reports → Sent messages, and clicking a name on Admin → Members opens everything about that person, including how messages reach them.
Prize pools follow sglive.speedgaming.org every 15 minutes and show beside each tournament on the event info list and the Watch page.
Best-of-3 and best-of-5 sets on Challonge and start.gg are booked as one match per game, and the set result goes to the bracket with its game score.
Staff can book a bracket match before its players are known ("Andy or Benny vs Cleo or Dash"), or create a placeholder match with just a title to hold a slot.
Players can tell staff they're running late from My Schedule or the stage reminder DM. The admin on duty hears about it; the opponent doesn't.
Dropping a player from a tournament forfeits or calls off their open matches in one go, and takes them off the Challonge bracket too.
Admin → Reports → Exports downloads a tournament's players and matches, and keeps every export for 3 days.
Challonge brackets can sync on a schedule, and a match someone already reported on Challonge or start.gg shows under Needs you to record in one tap.

Times now show on the clock your browser prefers: 9:30 PM if it uses 12-hour time, 21:30 if it uses 24-hour, and 9:30 PM when it doesn't say. If the guess is wrong, pick 12-hour or 24-hour under Profile → Time format, next to Timezone. Discord DMs follow your own Discord setting; email, Telegram and phone notifications, CSV exports and the Watch page use 12-hour.

Staff can call off a volunteer's shift from the Shift Board, for one person or the whole shift, even once it's started. The volunteer gets a DM saying they don't need to come (or can head out), skips check-in, and still gets full credit for the hours. Undo puts them back and tells them they're needed after all.

Admin → Reports → Staff / Crew Activity has a Crew by tournament table: how many matches each person commentated and tracked, grouped under each tournament. It only counts approved crew on finished matches that went to a stage, and exports to CSV.

Proctor Station finds a station: type a number like 7 in the search box and you'll see the unfinished matches with someone at station 7, their station lit up. On a phone the search box now sits above Filters instead of inside it.

The Watch page shows each stage as a tile with a live picture of its stream, and a bell on any upcoming match DMs you before it goes on stage. Staff can send signed-out viewers to a lightweight version so a crowd can't slow the app down.
Back and Forward step through tabs and views, a copied link opens the exact view you were on, and every section heading, match and shift has a link you can copy.

Match boards can fold any group (Finished starts folded), reset filters in one tap and approve crew in place. Big races show three names and "+N more" and finish without picking a winner, and Broadcast Techs get Proctor Station for stage matches.
My Schedule only shows what applies to you, and your Timeline adds community events and the crew slots still waiting on a stage.
The Capacity Forecast splits off-stream from on-stream players, keeps late matches on the clock, and leaves out tournaments played outside the tournament room.
Crew hear about a match only once it's on a stage, and the signup DM staff get updates itself when someone approves or withdraws the signup.
The side menu is bigger on a phone, with Home, Volunteer and Admin in a strip at the top that swaps the page list without leaving your page. Plenty of other screens got tidier on a phone too.
The event guide opens inside the app and has a Community events page, and staff can post a community event on another member's behalf.

Once a match starts, the schedule boards and My Schedule show when it actually started and when it should end (start plus the tournament's match length), turning amber if it runs over. Finished matches show their real start and finish.
The capacity forecast now expects a match to start about 15 minutes after its players check in, so it no longer frees their seats a quarter of an hour early.
Tournament admins and crew coordinators now see only their own tournaments on Reports → Staff / Crew Activity, including Crew by tournament. Staff still see the whole community.

When a player taps Running late on a match that's on a stage, the Broadcast Techs on shift hear about it too (every Broadcast Tech, if none is on shift). Staff can change or mute it on Admin › Notifications under "Player running late (Broadcast Techs)".

The match operations report now judges lateness by check-in as well as race start, shows how long matches take from check-in to start (split by staged and unstaged), and lists matches with impossible times, such as ones closed as played on Challonge, instead of letting them skew the averages.
On a phone, Proctor Station cards now show the tournament, bracket and game under the player names, like the desktop board.

A side the bracket hasn't decided yet ("TBD", "Winner of C", "Andy or Benny") now shows in grey italics on the match schedule, My Schedule, Not booked yet, the match details and the Watch page, so it no longer reads like a real player.
Matches under Up next on the run sheets now show an estimated end ("to ~22:25"): the booked time plus 15 minutes of setup plus the tournament's match length.

The fun facts under empty lists, loading spinners and the 404 page are about Hadestown this Saturday, switch to rollercoasters (Adventureland, Iowa included) at 6am Sunday, and go back to cats at 6am Monday. They're all listed at /facts, and the old /cat-facts link takes you there.

Players book a best-of-three's games one at a time, and in any order: "Waiting on you to pick a time" shows a row for each game left, with the deciding game marked "If needed". Schedules number the games by when they're played, so moving game 3 ahead of game 2 swaps their numbers.
Calling off one game of a best-of-three no longer takes the rest of the set with it.

Match cards on Match Schedule, Proctor Station, Event › Schedule and My Schedule have a new look. A coloured edge and a status word show each match's state at a glance (green live, amber late, blue checked in), and on a phone the time sits on its own line so names get the card's full width.
Every run sheet's Stage filter now has a "No stage" choice, so you can list just the matches that aren't on a stage, or mix it with a stage.

Checking in a match that's on a stage no longer asks for stations: one tap checks it in. Stage matches also stop showing "No stations yet" and "No station" tags, and the match sheet's checklist no longer flags their stations as missing.

On iPhone, links and buttons work on the first tap in the Home Screen app, turning on notifications no longer crashes Safari (Help now shows how to add Wizzrobe to the Home Screen), the bottom bar stays put, and older Safari gets an update message instead of a blank page.
The brief whole-app freezes during the event are much shorter, busy pages no longer stall everyone while they load, and schedules stop jumping back to page 1.

Resetting a bracket keeps the matches players already booked, a result already entered on Challonge is never overwritten, a result Challonge drops gets retried, and re-matching an entrant moves their booked matches with them.
Booking a best-of-three Challonge matchup from your Home page now asks for a time for every game and books them all, instead of booking game 1 only and leaving nowhere to roll game 2's seed.
Reloading a page you opened from a Discord link no longer reopens the dialog or repeats "That request has already been dealt with."

Average match length on Reports and Insights skips matches that were finished hours late (over three times the tournament's match length) or show zero minutes, so one late Finish click no longer drags a tournament's average up.

On the narrowest phones, Proctor Station no longer squeezes a match's names and ADA note into a thin column when a Roll seed or Start button sits beside them. The button moves under the names instead.
Challonge sign-ins now renew a few days before they lapse, so Service Health only warns when a renewal actually fails, and start.gg no longer says a sign-in lapsed when nobody had used it that week.

Booking another game for two players who already have an unfinished Challonge or start.gg match now offers to count it as the next game of that set, ticked by default. Challonge and start.gg then get the set's result instead of game 1's. This works even after game 1 has been played.

When a result is corrected on Challonge or start.gg and a different player moves up, both players in the new matchup now get the "ready to schedule" message. Before, the player who'd been moved up by mistake got it and the right one heard nothing.

On a phone, the Match Schedule and Event › Schedule cards now say which game of a best-of-three it is ("Game 2 of 3"), like the desktop rows, and the estimated end time ("to ~12:00 PM") no longer runs into the text beside it.
Broadcast Techs on Proctor Station now see only matches on a stage, as intended, instead of every match.

spans.text: Wizzrobe runs the schedule for speedrun and randomizer events: matches, brackets, crew, volunteers, equipment and check-in, with Discord sign-in and notifications. Each community gets its own space, run by its own staff.
It's free software under the
GNU General Public License v3
, and the source is on
GitHub

/api/about.built_with_claude: Much of Wizzrobe's code was written with Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic. A person reviews every change before it ships, but if something looks wrong, tell us through Send Feedback or your community's staff.

spans.text: Wizzrobe runs schedules, brackets, crew and volunteers for speedrun and randomizer events. This page says what it keeps about you, who can see it, who else it goes to, and how to get it changed or removed. Each community on Wizzrobe is run by its own staff, who decide how they use what you share with their community.
What we collect
When you sign in with Discord, Wizzrobe asks Discord for your basic profile only (the
identify
permission) and keeps your Discord ID, username and avatar. It doesn't keep your Discord password or your sign-in token, and it can't read your messages or servers.
Everything else is something you, or a community's staff, add:

items.text: Your profile:
a display name, pronouns and timezone.
Linked accounts

you choose to connect: Twitch, racetime.gg, Challonge, start.gg and Matcherino. We keep each account's ID and username, not its password or sign-in token, and you can unlink any of them from your profile.
Notification settings:

an email address and a Telegram chat, only if you turn those on, and a push subscription for each device you allow notifications on (with a short description of the browser, so you can tell your devices apart).
Event activity:
matches you play or crew, results and times, comments, reschedule requests, availability, tournament sign-ups, volunteer shifts, equipment you lend or borrow, and feedback you send.
Emergency contact and accessibility requests
, if you give them. These are only visible to the community's staff, and every time staff open your emergency contact you can see that they did.
Event check-in:

if a community sells badges through Matcherino, staff import its roster (name, Matcherino account and the Discord or Twitch account used to buy) to check you in. We drop the buyer's email, phone, address and payment details when we import it.

spans.text: Some people get an account before they ever sign in: a community can bring players in from the SpeedGaming schedule, a start.gg bracket, or its Discord server's roles. Those accounts hold the name and Discord ID those services published.
How the app uses cookies
Wizzrobe sets three cookies, all for running the app, none for advertising:

items.text: session
keeps you signed in, for 90 days after your last visit.
wiz_tz
remembers your device's timezone, so times show in your local time.
wiz_dark
remembers whether you picked dark mode.

spans.text: The app also records which pages and buttons get used (never what you type into them), tied to your account if you're signed in. Staff read it to learn which parts of the app people use. We don't store your IP address in the database.
Who can see it

items.text: Anyone
, signed in or not, can see schedules, brackets, results and the names of the players in them.
Members of your community
can see what the app shows on its schedule and crew pages, such as who's crewing a match.
Your community's staff and volunteers
can see what you've shared with that community, to run the event. Staff also see a log of changes made in the app.
Staff of other communities can't
see what you've shared with a community they don't run.

spans.text: We don't sell your information or use it for advertising.
Services we share it with
Wizzrobe hands the minimum each service needs to do its job:

items.text: Discord
, for sign-in, direct messages, server roles and event listings.
SendGrid
, to send email, if you turn email on.
Telegram
, to send messages, if you connect it.
Your browser's push service
(Google, Apple or Mozilla), to deliver notifications to devices you allow.
Sentry
, which receives error reports and performance data to help us fix problems. A report can include your Discord ID and username.
racetime.gg, Twitch, Challonge, start.gg and Matcherino
, when you link those accounts or a community uses them for its tournaments.
Webhooks and AI assistants a community's staff connect
, which receive the community's event data. Webhooks include the username of whoever made a change.

spans.text: Where it's stored

Your information is stored on servers in the United States, and the services above process it in the United States too. If you use Wizzrobe from outside the US, your information is transferred to and stored there.
How long we keep it

We keep your account and activity for as long as Wizzrobe runs your community's events, so past results and schedules stay accurate. You can remove your email, Telegram, push devices, linked accounts, emergency contact, accessibility request and availability yourself at any time from your profile. Emergency contacts and accessibility requests belong to one event: 30 days after staff archive that event, they're deleted.
The change log and usage records keep a copy of your username even after your account is gone, so the history of an event stays readable.
Your choices
To see what we hold about you, correct it, or have your account deleted, use
Send Feedback

in the side menu when you're signed in. If you can't sign in, ask your community's staff on their Discord server. Leaving a community removes your emergency contact and closes any accessibility request you had open there.
Children
Wizzrobe isn't meant for children under 13, and we don't knowingly keep information about them. If you think a child has signed up, tell us through Send Feedback and we'll remove the account.
Changes to this policy
When this policy changes, the date at the top of the page changes with it, and a bigger change gets a line on
What's new

Anatomy: Cats have 32 muscles in each ear and can rotate them 180 degrees.
Cats cannot taste sweetness — they lack the gene for sweet receptors.
A cat's nose print is as unique as a human fingerprint.
Cats have a third eyelid (nictitating membrane) rarely visible in healthy cats.
Cats have a free-floating clavicle, letting them squeeze through any gap their head fits through.
A cat's heart beats 140–220 bpm — roughly twice as fast as a human's.
Senses: A cat's field of vision is about 200 degrees — wider than a human's 180.
Cats need about one-sixth as much light as we do to see.
The eyeshine is a mirror called the tapetum lucidum, bouncing light back through the retina.
Cats are nearsighted: sharp up close, blurry past about 20 feet.
Cats see blues and yellows well and reds poorly — red-green colour blindness, not black and white.
Cat hearing reaches 64 kHz, nearly two octaves above the human ceiling and a full octave above a dog's.
Motion and balance: A cat can jump up to six times its own body length in a single leap.
The righting reflex works from as little as a foot of fall and is fully developed by seven weeks.
A falling cat rotates front half then back half, using its own inertia — no push-off required.
A falling cat tops out near 60 mph, half a human's, and spreads out like a parachute.
A 1987 study of 132 cats that fell from windows found those dropping past seven storeys were often less hurt.
Domestic cats sprint at around 30 mph in short bursts.
Sleep and grooming: Cats sleep 12–16 hours a day, among the sleepiest mammals on Earth.
A cat spends about two-thirds of its life asleep — a 12-year-old cat has been awake for four years.
Cats are crepuscular, not nocturnal: dawn and dusk are the busy shifts.
Cats dream: Michel Jouvet's 1960s experiments had sleeping cats acting out hunts.
A cat nap really is short — bouts run 15 to 100 minutes.
Cats spend up to half their waking hours grooming.
How cats talk: Cats can make around 100 distinct vocalizations; dogs manage about 10.
Adult cats barely meow at each other. The meow is aimed at humans.
Kittens meow at their mothers, then mostly stop — except with us.
A cat's purr vibrates at 25–150 Hz, a frequency shown to aid bone healing.
Purring isn't only contentment; injured and frightened cats purr too.
The purr comes from laryngeal muscles twitching 25 to 150 times a second.
Behaviour: Kneading — making biscuits — is nursing behaviour that never got switched off.
Cats cover their waste to keep their scent off the radar of anything bigger.
Cats bring prey home as provisioning behaviour: you are a very bad hunter who must be fed.
The post-litter-box zoomies have a name in the literature: frenetic random activity periods.
A 2014 study of shelter cats found a cardboard box measurably lowered their stress.
A 2017 study found cats will sit in a square of tape on the floor — an outline is box enough.
Health and lifespan: The world's oldest cat, Creme Puff, lived to be 38 years and 3 days old.
Indoor cats typically live 12 to 18 years; outdoor cats average far less.
Cats are obligate carnivores — without taurine in the diet, the heart and retinas fail.
Paracetamol and ibuprofen are poisonous to cats; cats lack the liver enzyme to process them.
Every part of a true lily is lethal to cats, pollen included.
Onions, garlic, and chocolate are all toxic to cats.
Ailments, and the good news: Feline diabetes often goes into remission — a low-carb diet gets plenty of cats off insulin entirely.
Hyperthyroidism has an actual cure: one dose of radioactive iodine fixes around 95% of cats, once.
Chronic kidney disease is manageable rather than terminal — caught early, cats live years on diet and fluids.
GS-441524 turned FIP from a death sentence into a course of treatment most cats walk away from.
Cats with FIV usually live a normal lifespan; it spreads through deep bite wounds, so a settled household stays safe.
Ringworm sounds dreadful and mostly clears on its own; treatment just shortens the wait.
Coats and genetics: Almost every calico and tortoiseshell cat is female — the orange gene rides on the X chromosome.
Male calicos are XXY, about one in 3,000, and nearly always sterile.
Roughly 80% of orange cats are male.
The gene behind orange fur, ARHGAP36, was finally pinned down in 2025.
Tortoiseshell patterning is X-inactivation made visible — a mosaic of two cell lineages.
Siamese points are temperature-sensitive albinism: pigment only forms where the body runs cool.
Breeds: The CFA recognises about 45 breeds; TICA recognises more than 70.
Most cats on Earth belong to no breed at all.
The Maine Coon is the largest domestic breed — the record is just under four feet nose to tail.
The Singapura is the smallest breed, often under five pounds.
The Sphynx isn't hairless; it's covered in fine down and needs regular baths.
Manx taillessness comes from a mutation that can also damage the spine.
Wild relatives: There are around 40 species in the cat family.
The domestic cat, Felis catus, descends from the African wildcat, Felis lybica.
A 2007 study traced every domestic cat to five maternal lineages from the Fertile Crescent.
The Scottish wildcat is critically endangered — mostly by breeding with house cats.
The black-footed cat is the deadliest cat alive: about 60% of its hunts succeed.
The rusty-spotted cat is the smallest wild cat, about the weight of a bag of sugar.
History: The oldest evidence of cats and people together is a 9,500-year-old joint burial in Cyprus.
Cats domesticated themselves, more or less, by moving in on the rodents in Neolithic grain stores.
Ancient Egyptians worshipped the cat goddess Bastet; harming a cat was punishable by death.
Herodotus wrote that Egyptian families shaved their eyebrows in mourning when a house cat died.
Egypt banned the export of cats, which did nothing to stop sailors taking them anyway.
In 1888, a shipment of hundreds of thousands of Egyptian cat mummies was sold in England as fertiliser.
Myth and superstition: The nine lives are regional: much of the Arabic- and Turkish-speaking world gives cats six or seven.
In Britain and Japan a black cat crossing your path is good luck. In much of the US it's the opposite.
The maneki-neko's raised right paw invites money; the left invites customers.
Freyja's chariot, in Norse myth, is pulled by cats.
Sailors prized polydactyl cats, believing the extra toes helped them keep their footing at sea.
The Cat Sìth of Highland folklore was a black cat with a white chest that could steal a soul.
Cats with jobs: Larry has been Chief Mouser to the Cabinet Office at 10 Downing Street since 2011.
The Hermitage Museum in St Petersburg has kept cats on staff since a 1745 decree; about 50 live there now.
New York's bodega cats are technically illegal and universally tolerated.
Tama, a calico, was stationmaster of Kishi Station in Japan and is credited with saving the line.
Stubbs the cat was honorary mayor of Talkeetna, Alaska, for 20 years.
Simon of HMS Amethyst is the only cat to receive the Dickin Medal for gallantry.
Famous cats: Grumpy Cat's expression came from feline dwarfism and an underbite.
Lil Bub was polydactyl, had osteopetrosis, and became a subject of published genetic research.
Maru, the Japanese cat who cannot resist a box, has been viewed hundreds of millions of times.
Orangey is the only cat to win two PATSY awards, including one for Breakfast at Tiffany's.
Choupette, Karl Lagerfeld's Birman, had her own staff.
Ernest Hemingway's Key West house still keeps about 60 cats, many of them polydactyl.
Records: A group of cats is called a clowder.
The loudest recorded purr belongs to Merlin, at 67.8 decibels — about as loud as a shower.
The longest jump by a cat is seven feet, set by Waffle the Warrior Cat.
The most toes on a cat is 28.
The longest fur on a cat measured just over nine inches.
The smallest adult cat on record stood about seven centimetres at the shoulder.
Words for cats: A group of kittens is a kindle.
A male cat is a tom; a female is a queen; a neutered male is a gib.
'Cat' comes from Late Latin cattus, and nearly every European language kept the root.
The ancient Egyptian word for cat was 'miu' — they named it after the noise.
An ailurophile loves cats. An ailurophobe does not.
Catgut was never made from cats. It's sheep intestine.
